summary: Specifies a new certificate type and two TLS extensions that let TLS and DTLS peers exchange raw public keys for authentication, without a full certificate.

plainLanguage.summary: A TLS handshake normally proves who the other end is by sending a certificate, a signed bundle of a public key and a great deal of other information. This document allows the handshake to carry only the public key, with nothing else attached, for cases where the key is already known by other means. The certificate machinery gets much simpler, but so does the security, unless something else ties the key to its owner.

questions: what is a raw public key in tls
how does tls use raw public keys
subtitle: Let TLS and DTLS peers authenticate with a bare public key instead of a full certificate.

tldr.problem: TLS normally ships public keys inside PKIX certificates checked against a certification authority, which is complex, large and wasteful when the certificate is self-signed or its other fields are never used.
tldr.mechanism: A new certificate type, RawPublicKey, carries just the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure. Two hello extensions, client_certificate_type and server_certificate_type, let each side negotiate which certificate types to use.
tldr.outcome: Keys are smaller and the code simpler, but authentication only works if the key is bound to its owner by some out-of-band method.

today: RFC 7250 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the way to exchange a raw public key in TLS and DTLS, registered as certificate type 2 in the TLS Certificate Types registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Traditionally, TLS client and server public keys are obtained in PKIX containers in-band as part of the TLS handshake procedure and are validated using trust anchors based on a certification authority. This method can add a complicated trust relationship that is difficult to validate. TLS is, however, also commonly used with self-signed certificates in smaller deployments where the self-signed certificates are distributed to all involved protocol endpoints out-of-band. This practice does, however, still require the overhead of the certificate generation even though none of the information found in the certificate is actually used.

Alternative methods are available that allow a TLS client or server to obtain the peer's public key. The TLS client can obtain the TLS server public key from a DNSSEC-secured resource record using DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities. The TLS client or server public key can be obtained from a PKIX certificate chain from an LDAP server or web page. Or the public key can be provisioned into the operating system firmware image and updated via software updates. Some smart objects use the UDP-based Constrained Application Protocol to interact with a web server to upload sensor data at regular intervals; CoAP can use DTLS for securing the client-to-server communication, and as part of the manufacturing process the embedded device may be configured with the address and the public key of a dedicated CoAP server, as well as a public and private key pair for the client itself.

This document introduces the use of raw public keys in TLS and DTLS. With raw public keys, only a subset of the information found in typical certificates is utilized, namely the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure of a PKIX certificate that carries the parameters necessary to describe the public key. Other parameters found in PKIX certificates are omitted. By omitting various certificate-related structures, the resulting raw public key is kept fairly small in comparison to the original certificate, and the code to process the keys can be simpler. Only a minimalistic ASN.1 parser is needed; code for certificate path validation and other PKIX-related processing is not required. The SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure is still in an ASN.1 format. To further reduce the size of the exchanged information, this specification can be combined with the TLS Cached Info extension, which enables TLS peers to exchange just fingerprints of their public keys.

The mechanism defined herein only provides authentication when an out-of-band mechanism is also used to bind the public key to the entity presenting the key.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates carry a lot of information that a small deployment never uses: names, validity dates, chains, signatures. This document says you may skip all of that and send only the public key itself. The code on the device then only has to read a small ASN.1 structure rather than run a whole certificate validation path. The catch, stated at the end of the section, is that nothing in the handshake itself says whose key it is.

sections.title: The Raw Public Key Extension
sections.content:
This specification uses raw public keys whereby the already available encoding used in a PKIX certificate in the form of a SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure is reused. To carry the raw public key within the TLS handshake, the Certificate payload is used as a container. The Certificate structure is an adaptation of its original form in TLS 1.2, and selects on the certificate type: the RawPublicKey case carries an ASN.1_subjectPublicKeyInfo, and the X.509 case carries the usual ASN.1Cert certificate_list.

The SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure is defined in Section 4.1 of RFC 5280 and not only contains the raw keys, such as the public exponent and the modulus of an RSA public key, but also an algorithm identifier, which can also include parameters. The SubjectPublicKeyInfo value in the Certificate payload MUST contain the DER encoding of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo, so the structure also contains length information. The structure is a SEQUENCE holding an AlgorithmIdentifier and a subjectPublicKey BIT STRING, and the AlgorithmIdentifier is a SEQUENCE holding an algorithm OBJECT IDENTIFIER and optional parameters.

The algorithm identifiers are Object Identifiers. RFC 3279 and RFC 5480, for example, define the object identifiers for RSA, the Digital Signature Algorithm and the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm. The list is not exhaustive, and more object identifiers may be defined in future RFCs.

The extension format for extended client and server hellos, which uses the extension_data field, is used to carry the ClientCertTypeExtension and the ServerCertTypeExtension structures. The CertificateType structure is an enum with values taken from the TLS Certificate Types subregistry. The client_certificate_type extension carries a list of certificate types in the client hello and a single type in the server hello, and the server_certificate_type extension does the same for server certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The key is sent in the same place a certificate would be sent, so nothing else in the handshake changes. The container simply has a new case in it that means a raw key instead of a certificate. The key itself is the same ASN.1 structure that sits inside a certificate, so the algorithm and the key bits are all still there, just without the surrounding certificate.

sections.title: How the Two Sides Agree
sections.content:
In order to indicate the support of raw public keys, clients include the client_certificate_type and/or the server_certificate_type extensions in an extended client hello message. The client_certificate_type extension in the client hello indicates the certificate types the client is able to provide to the server when requested using a certificate_request message. The server_certificate_type extension in the client hello indicates the types of certificates the client is able to process when provided by the server in a subsequent certificate payload. Both extensions sent in the client hello each carry a list of supported certificate types, sorted by client preference, and when the client supports only one certificate type it is a list containing a single element.

The client MUST omit certificate types from the client_certificate_type extension if it does not possess the corresponding raw public key or certificate, or if it is not configured to use one with the given TLS server. If the client has no remaining certificate types other than the default X.509 type, it MUST omit the client_certificate_type extension altogether. It MUST likewise omit certificate types from the server_certificate_type extension if it is unable to process the corresponding raw public key or other certificate type, and omit the whole extension if only the default X.509 type remains.

If the server receives a client hello that contains the extensions, three outcomes are possible. The server does not support the extension, in which case it returns the server hello without the extensions defined here. The server supports the extension but has no certificate type in common with the client, in which case it terminates the session with a fatal alert of type unsupported_certificate. Or the server supports the extensions and has at least one certificate type in common with the client, and the processing rules apply.

If the server wants to request a certificate from the client it MUST include the client_certificate_type extension in the server hello, and the value conveyed MUST be selected from one of the values provided in the client_certificate_type extension sent in the client hello. The server MUST also include a certificate_request payload. If the server does not send a certificate_request payload, or none of the certificates supported by the client match the server-supported certificate types, then the client_certificate_type payload in the server hello MUST be omitted.

If the client hello indicates support of raw public keys in the server_certificate_type extension and the server chooses to use raw public keys, then the TLS server MUST place the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure into the Certificate payload, and indicates the certificate type carried in the Certificate payload with the server_certificate_type extension. This additional indication avoids parsing ambiguities, since the Certificate payload may contain either the X.509 certificate or a SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure. Only a single value is permitted in the server_certificate_type extension when carried in the server hello.

No new cipher suites are required to use raw public keys: all existing cipher suites that support a key exchange method compatible with the defined extension can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The client lists, in preference order, the kinds of key it can send and the kinds it can accept. The server picks one of the client's choices and says which one it picked, so both sides know what the Certificate payload holds. If the client offers only the default X.509 type, it leaves the extension out entirely. If the server understands the extension but the two sides share no type at all, the server ends the connection with a fatal alert.

sections.title: Client and Server Authentication
sections.content:
When the TLS server has specified RawPublicKey as the client_certificate_type, authentication of the TLS client to the TLS server is supported only through authentication of the received client SubjectPublicKeyInfo via an out-of-band method. When the TLS server has specified RawPublicKey as the server_certificate_type, authentication of the TLS server to the TLS client is supported only through authentication of the received client SubjectPublicKeyInfo via an out-of-band method.

The certificate itself is what ties a public key to a name, and that is exactly what a raw public key does not have. The RFC therefore requires that something outside the handshake already says which key belongs to which party. DANE is one such approach: it publishes the key in a DNSSEC-signed record. Pre-configured keys are another: they are written into the device at manufacture time. The RFC notes that pre-configured keys are not suitable for a generic web-based e-commerce environment, but are a reasonable approach for many smart object deployments where there is a close relationship between the software running on the device and the server-side communication endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: Both directions are the same. A certificate says whose key it is; a raw key does not, so the two ends have to already know that some other way. The RFC names two: a key published in a DNSSEC-signed record, and a key written into the device before it ships. The second suits a sensor talking to one known server, and does not suit the open web.

sections.title: Example Exchanges
sections.content:
The first example shows a TLS client that can receive and validate a raw public key from the server but is unable to process other certificate types sent by the server. It has no credentials at the TLS layer it could send to the server, so it omits the client_certificate_type extension and populates only the server_certificate_type extension with the raw public key type. When the server receives the client hello it processes the extension, and since it has a raw public key it indicates that it has chosen to place the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure into the Certificate payload. The client uses this raw public key in the TLS handshake together with an out-of-band validation technique, such as DANE, to verify it.

The second example shows a TLS client and server both using raw public keys, which the document gives as one of the use cases envisioned for smart object networking. The client is an embedded device configured with a raw public key for use with TLS and also able to process a raw public key sent by the server, so it indicates both capabilities. The server fulfils the request, indicates this via the RawPublicKey value in the server_certificate_type payload, and provides a raw public key in the Certificate payload back to the client. The server demands client authentication, includes a certificate_request, and the client_certificate_type payload indicates that the server accepts a raw public key. The client, which has a raw public key pre-provisioned, returns it in the Certificate payload to the server.

The third example combines a raw public key and an X.509 certificate. The client uses a raw public key for client authentication and the server provides an X.509 certificate. The exchange starts with the client indicating its ability to process an X.509 certificate, an OpenPGP certificate, or a raw public key if provided by the server, and it prefers a raw public key because the RawPublicKey value precedes the other values in the server_certificate_type vector. The server chooses to provide its X.509 certificate and indicates that choice. For client authentication, the server indicates that it has selected the raw public key format and requests a certificate from the client, and the client provides a raw public key after receiving and processing the TLS server hello message.
sections.plainLanguage: Three worked exchanges. A client that only understands raw keys talks to a server that has one. A sensor and a server both use raw keys, which is the smart-object case the document has in mind. And a mixed case where the server uses an ordinary certificate while the client authenticates with a bare key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The transmission of raw public keys provides benefits by lowering the over-the-air transmission overhead, since raw public keys are naturally smaller than an entire certificate. There are also advantages from a code-size point of view for parsing and processing these keys. The cryptographic procedures for associating the public key with the possession of a private key also follow standard procedures.

However, the main security challenge is how to associate the public key with a specific entity. Without a secure binding between identifier and key, the protocol will be vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. This document assumes that such binding can be made out-of-band, and lists a few examples. DANE offers one such approach. In order to address these vulnerabilities, specifications that make use of the extension need to specify how the identifier and public key are bound. In addition to ensuring the binding is done out-of-band, an implementation also needs to check the status of that binding.

If public keys are obtained using DANE, these public keys are authenticated via DNSSEC. Using pre-configured keys is another out-of-band method for authenticating raw public keys. While pre-configured keys are not suitable for a generic web-based e-commerce environment, such keys are a reasonable approach for many smart object deployments where there is a close relationship between the software running on the device and the server-side communication endpoint. Regardless of the chosen mechanism for out-of-band public key validation, an assessment of the most suitable approach has to be made prior to the start of a deployment to ensure the security of the system.

An attacker might try to influence the handshake exchange to make the parties select different certificate types than they would normally choose. For this attack, the attacker must actively change one or more handshake messages. If this occurs, the client and server will compute different values for the handshake message hashes, and as a result the parties will not accept each other's Finished messages. Without the master secret, the attacker cannot repair the Finished messages, so the attack will be discovered.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole security story rests on the binding between a key and its owner, and the RFC is explicit that this must come from outside the handshake and must be checked. It also answers the obvious attack of tampering with the type negotiation: changing a handshake message makes the two sides compute different transcript hashes, so the Finished messages do not match and the connection fails. The attacker cannot fix that without the session secret.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has registered a new value in the TLS Certificate Types subregistry of the Transport Layer Security Extensions registry: value 2, Raw Public Key, with reference RFC 7250.

IANA has allocated two new TLS extensions, client_certificate_type and server_certificate_type, from the TLS ExtensionType Values subregistry defined in TLS 1.2. These extensions are used in both the client hello message and the server hello message. The new extension types are used for certificate type negotiation, and the values carried in these extensions are taken from the TLS Certificate Types subregistry.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA records a new certificate type with the number 2, called Raw Public Key, and two new extension codes, one for the client's certificate and one for the server's. Both extensions carry numbers from the same certificate type registry, so any future type can be negotiated the same way.
